title: Practice Set 8 — Dataflows Gen2: Low-Code Transformations
description: Decide when to use a Dataflow Gen2 versus a notebook for NordGrid's transformations, order Power Query transformation steps correctly, predict the row and column count after applying a sequence of steps, choose the correct dataflow destination for each output type, and write the PySpark equivalent of NordGrid's substation reference refresh dataflow — proving the student understands what the dataflow's visual steps actually do under the hood.
version: authored 2026-04-06, targets Microsoft Fabric GA 2025+ / PySpark 3.5+

metadata.scenarioScale: 500K meters, 4 regions, single team, 3 medallion workspaces
metadata.foundationException: Not applied. F8 is Essential Operations phase. Dataflows Gen2 are configured visually in Power Query Online — there is no PySpark API for them, and the practice environment has no Power Query runtime. Tasks 1-4 use templates to test the conceptual decisions a junior engineer makes when building or reviewing a dataflow: when to choose a dataflow over a notebook, what order to apply transformation steps, what output a sequence of steps produces, and where to send the result. The synthesis task (F8-task-05) writes a PySpark pipeline that performs the EXACT operations a Power Query dataflow would perform for NordGrid's substation reference refresh — read source, rename columns, filter rows, change types, and write to a Lakehouse table. This tests whether the student understands what the dataflow's visual steps actually do, which is the bedrock requirement of the Dataflow vs Notebook decision (Lesson 9). Task type mix (2 concept_identification + 2 output_prediction + 1 synthesis_pipeline) is within §4.2 per-type limits.

datasets.description: NordGrid substation data as it arrives from the external operations database — 10 rows with the SOURCE column names (sub_id, sub_name, cap_mw, status). 8 substations are active, 2 are decommissioned (SUB-07 Kristiansand Solar, SUB-09 Alesund Old Plant). The Silver target schema uses different column names: substation_id, substation_name, capacity_mw. Used by the synthesis task to test the rename + filter + type cast + write sequence that the substation refresh dataflow performs.

columns.name: status
columns.description: active or decommissioned; filter to active before writing

description.context: Dataflow Gen2 vs Notebook is a sweet-spot decision, not a winner-takes-all. DATAFLOW Gen2 wins when: data is SMALL (a few thousand rows), transformations are COLUMN-LEVEL (rename, retype, filter, simple merge), the team prefers low-code, and the source has a Power Query CONNECTOR (SharePoint, REST, common DBs). NOTEBOOK wins when: data is LARGE (hundreds of thousands of rows or more), transformations are COMPLEX (composite-key dedup, schema-enforcement on real volume, UDFs, custom Python libraries from PyPI like scikit-learn), or the workload integrates with an existing PySpark codebase. The discriminator is NOT the workload's nominal complexity — even simple operations on big data favor the Notebook because PySpark scales; Dataflows do not.
description.task: For each NordGrid transformation, choose the correct tool.
description.validationHint: Dataflow for: small reference tables, simple column-level operations, low-code preference, business analyst contributors. Notebook for: large data, complex logic, PySpark libraries, schema enforcement on production-scale data, deduplication on composite keys, custom UDFs.

fields.label: Refresh NordGrid's substation reference table (200 rows) from an external SQL database. The transformation: rename two columns, change one type, filter to active substations, write to a Silver Lakehouse table. The data team prefers low-code.
options: Dataflow Gen2 — 200 rows, column-level rename/retype/filter, low-code preferred. Every signal points to Dataflow. Textbook fit.
Notebook — every NordGrid transformation should use PySpark for codebase consistency, regardless of size or complexity.
Both — build it twice (Dataflow and Notebook) so the team can compare results and have redundancy.
Neither — refresh manually each week through a portal CSV upload.
fields.correctAnswer: Dataflow Gen2 — 200 rows, column-level rename/retype/filter, low-code preferred. Every signal points to Dataflow. Textbook fit.
fields.rationale: Small + column-level + low-code preference = Dataflow Gen2. The most common Junior confusion is over-applying 'consistency' to mean 'always Notebook'; consistency is good but applying the wrong tool to a 200-row column-level transformation just to keep one tool in use is a tax, not a benefit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Ignores every signal favoring Dataflow.

Option C: Doubles maintenance burden.

Option D: Manual refresh is unsustainable.

fields.label: Transform 500,000 daily meter readings: enforce an explicit StructType schema, filter null daily_kw, filter daily_kw outside (0, 10000), deduplicate on the composite key (meter_id, date), and write a partitioned Delta table.
options: Dataflow Gen2 — visual transformations are easier to maintain than code; Power Query handles every step listed.
Notebook — 500K rows, explicit StructType, composite-key dedup, partitioned Delta write. Every characteristic falls outside Dataflow's sweet spot. PySpark is the right tool.
Either tool — Dataflow and Notebook handle the same operations with equivalent performance at this scale.
A pipeline with no transformation activity — let the orchestrator handle everything via Copy with column mapping.
fields.correctAnswer: Notebook — 500K rows, explicit StructType, composite-key dedup, partitioned Delta write. Every characteristic falls outside Dataflow's sweet spot. PySpark is the right tool.
fields.rationale: Large data + complex logic (composite-key dedup, schema-enforced StructType, partitioned Delta write) = Notebook. The most common Junior confusion is choosing the visual tool because 'easier to maintain'; on production-scale data with complex logic, the Notebook is BOTH more performant and clearer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Dataflows don't scale well to 500K with complex logic.

Option C: Different sweet spots; not equivalent.

Option D: Pipelines orchestrate, they don't transform.

fields.label: Filter and type-cast 500,000 NordGrid readings into a partitioned Delta table — same scale as Module F6's Silver pipeline, but with simpler logic (no dedup, just filter and cast).
options: Dataflow Gen2 — operations are simple and column-level; Dataflow's sweet spot, regardless of row count.
Notebook — 500K rows + partitioned Delta write + integrates with the existing Silver Notebook codebase. SCALE pushes the choice past Dataflow's sweet spot even when LOGIC looks simple.
Either tool — at this row count the choice is purely stylistic.
Power BI Dataflow — Power BI's older Dataflow handles million-row transformations natively and should be used for any production data.
fields.correctAnswer: Notebook — 500K rows + partitioned Delta write + integrates with the existing Silver Notebook codebase. SCALE pushes the choice past Dataflow's sweet spot even when LOGIC looks simple.
fields.rationale: Even simple operations on 500K rows favor the Notebook because PySpark scales naturally and Dataflows do not. The most common Junior confusion is picking by LOGIC complexity alone; SCALE is an equally important axis, and 500K is past Dataflow's comfort zone.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Dataflows underperform at 500K.

Option C: Scale is not stylistic.

Option D: Power BI Dataflow is a different older product.

fields.label: Refresh NordGrid's region lookup table (4 rows: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST with display names and country codes) from a SharePoint list maintained by the operations team. Operations team members occasionally update the list themselves and want to see the change reflected in Fabric without engineering involvement.
options: Dataflow Gen2 — SharePoint is a first-class Power Query connector, 4 rows is tiny, visual interface lets ops team trace the logic. Every signal favors Dataflow.
Notebook — even tiny transformations should use PySpark for codebase consistency.
Manual portal upload each time the SharePoint list changes; engineer copies the file when ops team requests.
An Azure Function triggered by SharePoint webhook to push updates into Fabric in real time.
fields.correctAnswer: Dataflow Gen2 — SharePoint is a first-class Power Query connector, 4 rows is tiny, visual interface lets ops team trace the logic. Every signal favors Dataflow.
fields.rationale: Tiny + SharePoint source + visual transparency for non-engineers = Dataflow Gen2. Power Query's connector ecosystem is one of Dataflow's strongest assets. The most common Junior confusion is reaching for Notebook by default; SharePoint integration is exactly what Dataflows excel at.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Ignores connector strength and scale.

Option C: Manual upload is fragile.

Option D: Over-engineering for a 4-row lookup.

fields.label: Apply a custom Python machine-learning library (scikit-learn) to NordGrid's meter readings to detect anomalies. The library is available on PyPI, the model needs to be trained once and applied to incoming readings via a UDF.
options: Dataflow Gen2 — Power Query has built-in ML support and can pip-install PyPI libraries on dataflow refresh.
Notebook — PyPI library + custom Python + UDF application = firmly Notebook territory. Power Query cannot run scikit-learn or invoke Python UDFs.
Both — train the model in a Notebook, then apply via UDF in a Dataflow that calls the trained model.
Neither — anomaly detection always belongs to Real-Time Intelligence; batch ML is not a Notebook or Dataflow workload.
fields.correctAnswer: Notebook — PyPI library + custom Python + UDF application = firmly Notebook territory. Power Query cannot run scikit-learn or invoke Python UDFs.
fields.rationale: Anything involving custom Python libraries or UDFs is Notebook territory — Dataflow's transformation language (Power Query M) cannot import or invoke arbitrary Python. The most common Junior confusion is hoping Dataflows can host ML; they can't.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Power Query has no built-in ML/scikit-learn integration.

Option C: Dataflow can't invoke a trained scikit-learn model.

Option D: RTI is for streaming; batch ML lives in Notebooks.

tasks.title: Order the Power Query Transformation Steps

description.context: Power Query's Applied Steps execute in the order they appear, top to bottom. Each step transforms the output of the previous step, so dependencies dictate ordering. Three universal rules: (1) CONNECT TO SOURCE must come first — every later step needs data to operate on. (2) SET DESTINATION must come last — once you write out, you can't transform further. (3) Between those, a step that REFERENCES a column needs that column to still exist with the name it expects: e.g. filter on 'status' must come BEFORE remove 'status' column; change-type on 'capacity_mw' must come AFTER rename 'cap_mw' to 'capacity_mw' (otherwise the column doesn't exist by that name yet). Reordering Applied Steps is the most common bug-source in Power Query: a step that worked in isolation breaks when you reorder.
description.task: Place the 6 steps in the correct execution order for NordGrid's substation refresh dataflow.
description.validationHint: Two rules govern the ordering. First, you cannot transform data you have not yet read — Connect to Source must come first. Second, the destination must come last. Between those, dependencies decide the order: filtering by 'status' must happen BEFORE removing the status column, and changing the capacity_mw type must happen AFTER renaming cap_mw → capacity_mw (or use the original column name and rename later — but the rename-first ordering is the conventional Power Query pattern).

fields.label: What is the FIRST step in the dataflow?
options: A. Filter Rows — start by narrowing the input as early as possible to reduce data volume in subsequent steps.
B. Connect to Source — every transformation needs data; the connect step is what loads it. Always first.
C. Set Destination — writing the empty target out first reserves the destination so subsequent steps can target it.
E. Rename Columns — establish the target schema before any data is loaded so subsequent steps know what to expect.
fields.correctAnswer: B. Connect to Source — every transformation needs data; the connect step is what loads it. Always first.
fields.rationale: Connect to Source is universally first because every subsequent step transforms its output. The most common Junior confusion is reordering for performance reasons; Power Query's pushdown handles that automatically and the logical order must still start with Connect.
fields.distractorRationale: Options A, C, E: All assume data is already loaded. Without Connect, those steps have nothing to operate on.

fields.label: What is the LAST step in the dataflow?
options: A. Filter Rows — finish by filtering the output to only the rows the destination will accept.
C. Set Destination — writing the transformed data out is the terminal step; nothing transforms data already written.
F. Remove Columns — finalize the schema as the last step before the dataflow auto-writes.
D. Change Type — finalize types as the last step so the destination receives correctly-typed data.
fields.correctAnswer: C. Set Destination — writing the transformed data out is the terminal step; nothing transforms data already written.
fields.rationale: Set Destination is always last because there's nothing to transform AFTER you write. The most common Junior confusion is treating Destination as just another step that can be reordered; it's a TERMINAL step by design.
fields.distractorRationale: Options A, D, F: All are transformation steps that can be reordered among themselves but never AFTER the destination.

fields.label: Filter Rows (A) keeps only rows where status = 'active'. Remove Columns (F) drops the status column. Which must come first?
options: Filter Rows (A) before Remove Columns (F) — the filter REFERENCES the status column, so the column must still exist when the filter runs. Then drop status.
Remove Columns (F) before Filter Rows (A) — Power Query requires column removal before any filter step.
Order does not matter — Power Query analyzes the steps and applies them in the optimal order automatically.
They can run in parallel — independent steps execute concurrently in modern Power Query.
fields.correctAnswer: Filter Rows (A) before Remove Columns (F) — the filter REFERENCES the status column, so the column must still exist when the filter runs. Then drop status.
fields.rationale: A step that references column X needs column X to exist at that point in the pipeline. Filter on status must precede Remove status. The most common Junior confusion is hoping Power Query reorders steps for you; Applied Steps run literally in the listed order.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a Power Query rule that doesn't exist.

Option C: Power Query does not auto-reorder.

Option D: Steps execute sequentially, not in parallel.

fields.label: Rename Columns (E) renames cap_mw → capacity_mw. Change Type (D) changes capacity_mw from text to decimal. Which must come first?
options: Change Type (D) before Rename (E) — type definitions are conceptually before names; types are intrinsic, names are labels.
Rename (E) before Change Type (D) — D's expression references 'capacity_mw' which only exists AFTER the rename. Step order tracks the column name in the expression.
Order does not matter — Power Query auto-references both the old name (cap_mw) and the new name (capacity_mw).
Both must happen in the same step using a combined Rename-and-Type transformation.
fields.correctAnswer: Rename (E) before Change Type (D) — D's expression references 'capacity_mw' which only exists AFTER the rename. Step order tracks the column name in the expression.
fields.rationale: The Change Type step's expression names 'capacity_mw' — that name only exists after the rename. Step order matches the literal column names referenced in each expression. The most common Junior confusion is hoping Power Query auto-tracks renames; it tracks the EXPLICIT name written in each step.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: No 'types before names' rule.

Option C: No auto-reference for renamed columns.

Option D: Each transformation is its own Applied Step.

fields.label: Putting it all together, which sequence is the correct order for all 6 steps?
options: B, E, D, A, F, C — Connect, Rename, Change Type (on renamed col), Filter (status still present), Remove status, Set Destination. Every dependency satisfied.
B, A, F, E, D, C — Connect, Filter, Remove status, Rename, Change Type, Destination. (Filter before rename uses old name; type change after status removal works only if capacity_mw stays.)
B, C, A, E, D, F — Connect, Set Destination second, then transform. Writes empty target, then transforms after.
C, B, A, E, D, F — Set Destination first, then Connect, then transformations. Target reserved before reading source.
fields.correctAnswer: B, E, D, A, F, C — Connect, Rename, Change Type (on renamed col), Filter (status still present), Remove status, Set Destination. Every dependency satisfied.
fields.rationale: The order satisfies all three universal rules: Connect first, Destination last, every column reference still exists at its step. Rename precedes Change Type (target column), Filter precedes Remove (status). The most common Junior confusion is missing one dependency; conjoining all three constraints fixes the unique answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Filter before Rename works for status but the type change happens after Filter referencing renamed column — works only because capacity_mw is preserved.

Option C: Set Destination second writes before transforming.

Option D: Inverts Connect and Destination.

description.context: Each Power Query transformation has predictable effects on shape: FILTER ROWS narrows row count, leaves columns unchanged. REMOVE COLUMNS narrows column count, leaves rows unchanged. RENAME COLUMNS is metadata only — same row count, same column count, just different name. CHANGE TYPE is per-cell and may transform values: text-to-number parses; decimal-to-whole-number TRUNCATES toward zero (it does NOT round, contrary to most languages' default). Tracing a sequence of these is just doing each effect in order against the running shape. The trick is keeping straight that Change Type CAN modify cell values (e.g. truncation), even though it doesn't change row or column counts.
description.task: Predict the output of the dataflow.
description.validationHint: Step 1 keeps only NORTH rows: rows 1, 2, 4, 7, 10 = 5 rows. Step 2 removes substation_id: 4 columns remain (meter_id, daily_kw, date, region). Step 3 renames daily_kw to kwh: still 4 columns. Step 4 truncates kwh values to integers (1200.5 → 1200, 1850.3 → 1850, etc.) but does not change the row or column count.

fields.label: After all 4 steps, how many rows are in the output?
fields.rationale: Only Step 1 (Filter Rows) changes the row count. It keeps NORTH rows: rows 1, 2, 4, 7, and 10 = 5 rows. Steps 2, 3, and 4 do not affect row count.

fields.label: After all 4 steps, how many columns are in the output?
fields.rationale: The input has 5 columns. Step 2 (Remove Columns) drops substation_id, leaving 4 columns. Step 3 (Rename Columns) and Step 4 (Change Type) modify column metadata but do not change the count.

fields.label: What are the column names in the final output, in order?
options: meter_id, daily_kw, date, region — substation_id removed (correct), but Rename was a metadata-only step that does not change column names visible in the schema.
meter_id, kwh, date, region — Step 2 removed substation_id and Step 3 renamed daily_kw to kwh. Both shape changes applied.
meter_id, daily_kw, date, region, substation_id — Remove Columns was a no-op because substation_id is still referenced by upstream metadata.
meter_id, kwh, date, region, substation_id — Rename applied; Remove was deferred until Set Destination, so substation_id is still present.
fields.correctAnswer: meter_id, kwh, date, region — Step 2 removed substation_id and Step 3 renamed daily_kw to kwh. Both shape changes applied.
fields.rationale: Apply each step in order: start with 5 columns, Remove drops substation_id (4 left), Rename changes daily_kw to kwh (still 4). The most common Junior confusion is hoping Rename is metadata-only that doesn't propagate; in Power Query, Rename does change the column name visible in subsequent steps and the destination.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Misses the rename effect.

Option C: Misses the remove effect.

Option D: Invents deferred removal.

fields.label: What is the kwh value for the row originally containing M-0004 (daily_kw 2100.7) after the type change to whole number?
options: 2101 — Power Query rounds to the nearest integer (banker's rounding for .5 ties).
2100 — Power Query TRUNCATES toward zero on decimal-to-whole-number cast. The .7 is dropped, not rounded.
2100.7 — Change Type only updates column metadata; values stay decimal. Whole-number is just a label.
Null — the cast fails because 2100.7 has a non-zero fractional part and the cell becomes null.
fields.correctAnswer: 2100 — Power Query TRUNCATES toward zero on decimal-to-whole-number cast. The .7 is dropped, not rounded.
fields.rationale: Power Query's decimal-to-whole-number transformation TRUNCATES (drops the fractional part toward zero) — it does NOT round. The most common Junior confusion is importing rounding intuition from most other languages; Power Query is a truncate-by-default ecosystem and 2100.7 becomes 2100, not 2101.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Power Query truncates, doesn't round.

Option C: Change Type does modify values for type-narrowing casts.

Option D: No cast failure for valid decimals.

description.context: Dataflow Gen2 destinations choose the downstream surface for the transformed output. Three core options: LAKEHOUSE TABLE (writes a Delta table in the Lakehouse Tables section; read-only via auto-generated SQL endpoint; suitable for downstream notebooks and analyst SELECTs). WAREHOUSE TABLE (writes a SQL-native table; supports full read-write T-SQL; suitable when analysts maintain the table via DML after the dataflow writes). EXTERNAL AZURE SQL DATABASE (writes outside Fabric to an external SQL store; suitable when downstream consumers live outside Fabric and need direct access). The discriminator is who reads/writes the table and where they live.
description.task: For each NordGrid dataflow output, select the correct destination.
description.validationHint: Lakehouse table: when downstream notebooks or the Lakehouse SQL endpoint will consume the data. Warehouse table: when analysts will INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE the data after the dataflow writes it. External Azure SQL: when the data must flow OUT of Fabric to a system that consumes it directly.

fields.label: NordGrid's substation reference table is refreshed daily. The output is consumed by NordGrid's Silver transformation notebook (which reads it from the Tables section) and by the SQL analytics endpoint for ad-hoc analyst queries. Nobody writes to this table after the dataflow.
options: Lakehouse table — read-only downstream (notebook + auto-generated SQL endpoint), no DML needed. Lakehouse table is the right destination.
Warehouse table — all SQL access in Fabric should go through a Warehouse for consistency.
External Azure SQL Database — share the substation table with downstream external systems for governance.
Bronze Lakehouse Files section — keep the refreshed data in raw form for reproducibility.
fields.correctAnswer: Lakehouse table — read-only downstream (notebook + auto-generated SQL endpoint), no DML needed. Lakehouse table is the right destination.
fields.rationale: When all downstream access is READ-ONLY (notebook + SQL endpoint), the Lakehouse table destination is the correct choice. The most common Junior confusion is over-applying 'SQL = Warehouse'; the Lakehouse SQL endpoint covers read-only SQL perfectly.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Endpoint covers reads; no Warehouse needed.

Option C: Ships data outside Fabric for no reason.

Option D: Refined Silver data in Bronze defeats the layering.

fields.label: NordGrid's reporting team receives a pre-computed monthly summary table from a dataflow. After the dataflow writes the table, the reporting team manually adds reconciliation rows and updates incorrect values via T-SQL — they need INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE access on the table.
options: Lakehouse table — the auto-generated SQL endpoint handles the analyst writes; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE work via the endpoint.
Warehouse table — full read-write T-SQL (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) is what the reporting team needs; only the Warehouse supports DML.
Files section — keep the summary as a raw CSV that analysts download and edit locally.
Power BI semantic model — analyst edits go through Power BI's visual editing, replacing SQL DML.
fields.correctAnswer: Warehouse table — full read-write T-SQL (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) is what the reporting team needs; only the Warehouse supports DML.
fields.rationale: DML requirement = Warehouse, every time. The Lakehouse SQL endpoint is READ-ONLY (covered in F4). The most common Junior confusion is hoping the endpoint can be 'unlocked' for writes; it cannot, by design.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Endpoint is read-only.

Option C: Files for analyst-edited summaries is a workflow downgrade.

Option D: Semantic models are query layers, not writable stores.

fields.label: NordGrid's compliance team maintains a separate Azure SQL Database that audits external regulatory submissions. A weekly dataflow extracts a slice of the Gold compliance table from Fabric and writes it to this external Azure SQL Database for the compliance team's external auditing tool.
options: Lakehouse table — keep all data in Fabric. The compliance tool can read Fabric Lakehouses via OneLake APIs.
Warehouse table — Fabric Warehouse is functionally equivalent to Azure SQL DB; same DML surface, same governance.
External Azure SQL Database — the consumer (compliance tool) lives OUTSIDE Fabric and reads Azure SQL natively. Destination matches consumer location.
OneLake shortcut to Azure SQL — create a shortcut so the compliance tool sees the data without the data physically leaving Fabric.
fields.correctAnswer: External Azure SQL Database — the consumer (compliance tool) lives OUTSIDE Fabric and reads Azure SQL natively. Destination matches consumer location.
fields.rationale: When downstream consumers live outside Fabric, write to an external destination so they can read it natively. The most common Junior confusion is conflating shortcuts (point Fabric AT external data) with destinations (write OUT to external systems); they're opposite directions.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Compliance tool isn't reading Fabric Lakehouse APIs.

Option B: Warehouse stays inside Fabric.

Option D: Shortcuts are inbound, not outbound.

fields.label: NordGrid's region lookup table (4 rows) refreshes weekly from a SharePoint list. Downstream consumers: notebooks reading region display names, and Power BI reports showing region filters. Nobody writes back to it.
options: Lakehouse table — read-only consumers (notebooks + Power BI Direct Lake), no downstream writes. Lakehouse covers both consumers natively.
Warehouse table — Power BI prefers a Warehouse for analytical performance; the Lakehouse SQL endpoint is too slow for BI.
External Azure SQL Database — SharePoint sources must round-trip through SQL before Power BI can consume them.
An Azure Function that proxies the SharePoint list to Fabric, refreshed in real time.
fields.correctAnswer: Lakehouse table — read-only consumers (notebooks + Power BI Direct Lake), no downstream writes. Lakehouse covers both consumers natively.
fields.rationale: Read-only + small + multi-consumer = Lakehouse table. Power BI reads Lakehouse tables natively via Direct Lake. The most common Junior confusion is hoping Power BI requires a Warehouse for performance; Direct Lake on Lakehouse Delta tables is the modern Fabric pattern.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Power BI doesn't require a Warehouse.

Option C: No round-trip-through-SQL requirement.

Option D: Over-engineering a simple lookup.

tasks.title: Build the PySpark Equivalent of NordGrid's Substation Refresh Dataflow

description.context:
NordGrid's substation reference refresh is built as a Dataflow Gen2 in production. But to prove you understand what the dataflow's visual steps are doing, your task is to write the PySpark equivalent. Each line of your code maps directly to one Power Query step. If you can write this PySpark version correctly, you understand the dataflow well enough to maintain it, debug it, and explain it to a junior teammate.

The substation source table arrives with the SOURCE column names (sub_id, sub_name, cap_mw, status) and contains 10 substations — 8 active, 2 decommissioned. Your task is to apply the 4 dataflow transformations in PySpark and write the result as a managed Delta table called substations_silver. The transformations:

  Step 1. Read F8_data_substations_source.csv (Connect to Source)
  Step 2. Rename columns: sub_id → substation_id, sub_name → substation_name, cap_mw → capacity_mw (Rename Columns)
  Step 3. Filter to rows where status equals 'active' (Filter Rows)
  Step 4. Drop the status column (no longer needed) — this is the Remove Columns step
  Step 5. Write the result as a managed table called substations_silver with mode='overwrite' using saveAsTable (Set Destination)
description.task: Build the full pipeline. Read the source CSV with header=True and inferSchema=True. Apply the 4 transformations in order. Write the result as a managed Delta table called substations_silver. After writing, read the table back into df_substations_silver and store the row count in silver_count. Then verify the rename and filter worked: store the column list in silver_columns, and store the count of any 'decommissioned' substations remaining (which should be 0) in decommissioned_remaining.
description.validationHint: Use withColumnRenamed (or .toDF) for the renames, .filter() for the active filter, .drop('status') for the column removal, and .write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('substations_silver') for the destination. Expected: silver_count = 8 (10 source minus 2 decommissioned), silver_columns has substation_id/substation_name/capacity_mw (no status, no sub_*), decommissioned_remaining = 0.

starterScaffold.content:
# F8 synthesis: write the PySpark equivalent of NordGrid's substation refresh dataflow.
# Each Power Query step maps to one PySpark operation. If you understand the dataflow,
# you can write this code. If you can write this code, you understand the dataflow.
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName('nordgrid-substation-refresh') \
    .master('local[*]') \
    .enableHiveSupport() \
    .getOrCreate()

print('Spark ready. Building substation refresh dataflow equivalent.')

# YOUR SOLUTION BELOW

# Step 1: Read F8_data_substations_source.csv (header=True, inferSchema=True)
#         Store in df_source.



# Step 2: Rename columns:
#         sub_id -> substation_id
#         sub_name -> substation_name
#         cap_mw -> capacity_mw
#         (Use withColumnRenamed three times, or chain.)
#         Store in df_renamed.



# Step 3: Filter to rows where status == 'active'.
#         Store in df_active.



# Step 4: Drop the 'status' column.
#         Store in df_final.



# Step 5: Write df_final as a managed table called 'substations_silver' with mode='overwrite'.
#         Then read it back into df_substations_silver.



# Compute verification values:
#   silver_count = row count of df_substations_silver
#   silver_columns = list of df_substations_silver column names
#   decommissioned_remaining = count of rows in df_substations_silver whose substation_id is
#                              one of the known decommissioned ids ('SUB-07', 'SUB-09').
#                              If your filter worked, this is 0.



# YOUR SOLUTION ABOVE

# Verification (do not modify)
print(f"Source rows: {df_source.count()}")
print(f"Silver rows: {silver_count}")
print(f"Silver columns: {silver_columns}")
print(f"Decommissioned remaining in Silver: {decommissioned_remaining}")
df_substations_silver.show()

assertions.description: df_source loaded with 10 rows from the source CSV
df_renamed has the new column names (substation_id, substation_name, capacity_mw, status)

tasks.partialCredit: 9 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/9 credit. A student who completes the source read, rename, and filter (steps 1-3) earns at least 3/9 even if the column drop or write fails.

conceptsCombined: Connecting to a source — equivalent to Power Query's 'Connect to Data Source' (Lesson 3)
Renaming columns — equivalent to Power Query's 'Rename Columns' transformation (Lesson 4)
Filtering rows by a status value — equivalent to Power Query's 'Filter Rows' transformation (Lesson 4)
Dropping a column — equivalent to Power Query's 'Remove Columns' transformation (Lesson 4)
Writing to a Lakehouse table destination — equivalent to Power Query's 'Set Destination' (Lesson 6)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This task is unusual: it tests F8 dataflow knowledge by asking the student to write code in PySpark. The pedagogical justification is in Lesson 9, which establishes the Dataflow vs Notebook decision framework. To make that decision well, the student must understand what each Power Query step DOES — which means they must be able to express the dataflow as code mentally. Writing the code makes that understanding concrete and auto-gradable. The 5 mapped concepts (one per dataflow step) cover Lessons 3, 4, and 6 — the core transformation lessons. A student who builds this pipeline correctly proves they understand both how a dataflow is structured AND how its operations map to PySpark equivalents — preparing them for the F9 SQL alternative and the F10 medallion synthesis.

selfCheck.foundationModuleException: Not applied. F8 is Essential Operations phase. Five tasks (the §2.2 minimum for junior). Task type mix is 2 concept_identification + 2 output_prediction + 1 synthesis_pipeline — within all §4.2 per-type limits. The synthesis task is the only code task, which is intentional: F8 has no PySpark API surface (Power Query is visual), so attempting more code tasks would mean teaching Power Query through code, which is awkward. The decision-and-prediction tasks fit the visual nature of dataflows.
selfCheck.theoryPracticeBoundary: The theory teaches Power Query Online's visual interface and walks through NordGrid's substation refresh as the running example in Lessons 4, 5, and 10. The practice tests application: Task 1 uses transformation scenarios beyond the substation example to force the Dataflow-vs-Notebook decision. Task 2 takes the substation refresh and scrambles its steps, requiring the student to reason about ordering rules. Task 3 uses a 10-row sample with different data than the theory's example to test step-by-step output prediction. Task 4 tests destination decisions across 4 different scenarios. Task 5 takes the same substation refresh from the theory and asks the student to build the PySpark equivalent — proving they understand what each visual step does.
selfCheck.crossModuleNotes: This practice set builds on multiple earlier modules. F4's Lakehouse vs Warehouse decision is reused in Task 4 (destination choice). F5's pre-configured spark and saveAsTable patterns are reused in Task 5. F6's transformation patterns (filter, rename, drop) are reused in Task 5 — the student writes the same operations in PySpark. F7's pipeline-vs-notebook distinction is implicit in Task 1 (Dataflow Gen2 is a third option alongside notebook and pipeline activities). None of these are tested in isolation — F8's testable concepts are the dataflow-specific ones: Power Query step ordering, Dataflow vs Notebook decision criteria, dataflow destinations, and the dataflow-to-PySpark equivalence. F9 and F10 concepts are not required.
selfCheck.datasetNotes: One small dataset (10 rows) used only by the synthesis task. The source uses SOURCE column names (sub_id, sub_name, cap_mw, status) — different from the Silver target — so the rename step is meaningful. 2 of 10 rows are decommissioned (SUB-07, SUB-09), so the filter step removes exactly 2 rows leaving 8. The arithmetic is deterministic: 10 source - 2 decommissioned = 8 silver rows.
